title: What Sellers Should Know About Buyer Repair Requests
content_html:
Once a buyer completes a home inspection, it's common for them to come back with a list of requested repairs or credits before agreeing to move forward. For sellers, this moment can feel tense — but understanding how the process works, what your options actually are, and how to respond thoughtfully can keep the transaction on track without giving away more than necessary.

Where Repair Requests Come From

In a typical California transaction, the purchase agreement includes an inspection contingency, which gives the buyer a defined period to investigate the property's condition. Contingencies in a California purchase agreement are the buyer's built-in protections — they allow the buyer to inspect, evaluate, and in many cases negotiate or walk away based on what they find.

After a general home inspection — and sometimes additional specialized inspections for items like roofing, pest activity, sewer lines, or pool equipment — the buyer's agent typically submits a written "Request for Repair" or similar form. This isn't a demand with automatic legal force; it's an opening position in a negotiation.

You Are Not Automatically Obligated to Make Repairs

A common misconception is that a seller must complete whatever a buyer requests after inspection. That isn't how it works. The inspection contingency generally exists to let the buyer decide whether to proceed with the purchase, not to compel the seller into a particular repair. As the seller, you generally have a few paths available once a repair request arrives:

  • Agree to make some or all of the requested repairs before closing, typically using licensed contractors and providing receipts or documentation.
  • Offer a credit at closing instead of completing repairs yourself, giving the buyer funds to address the items after they take ownership.
  • Negotiate a price reduction in lieu of repairs or credits.
  • Decline the request entirely, which may lead the buyer to proceed anyway, renegotiate, or exercise their contingency right to cancel.

Which path makes sense depends on the nature of the items raised, your timeline, your relationship with the buyer up to that point, and what else is happening in the local market.

Separating Safety and Material Defects From Cosmetic Wish Lists

Inspection reports often mix genuinely significant findings — a roof leak, outdated electrical panel, or active termite infestation — with minor or cosmetic observations that inspectors are trained to note but that don't meaningfully affect the home's safety or function. A buyer's initial repair request sometimes reflects the full report rather than a prioritized list.

It's worth reviewing the request item by item with your agent rather than reacting to the overall length of the list. Some items may already be known and reflected in your pricing. Others may be new information that changes the picture for both sides. Treating every line item with equal weight — whether that means fighting every one or agreeing to every one — rarely produces the best outcome for either party.

Your Disclosure Obligations Still Apply

Regardless of how you respond to the repair request itself, anything the inspection reveals about the property's condition generally needs to be reflected in your disclosures if it's a material fact affecting value or desirability. This is true even if the buyer doesn't ask you to fix it, and even if the sale ultimately doesn't close with this buyer. If you've already completed your seller disclosure requirements, a significant new finding from inspection may call for an amended or supplemental disclosure. Talk with your agent about how newly discovered conditions should be documented going forward, including for any future buyer if this transaction doesn't close.

Negotiating a Response

A few practical habits tend to serve sellers well when responding to a repair request:

  • Get contractor input before committing. A buyer's request may estimate a cost or scope that doesn't match what an actual licensed contractor would charge or recommend. Don't agree to a number you haven't verified.
  • Respond in writing, through the same contract process the request came through, so the negotiation is documented and both sides' agents are tracking the same terms.
  • Consider the credit-versus-repair tradeoff. A closing credit avoids the hassle of coordinating contractors on a deadline, but some buyers' lenders place limits on how large a seller credit can be, and some buyers prefer repairs actually completed rather than cash.
  • Keep your timeline in mind. Contingency periods in California transactions are typically time-bound, so a drawn-out back-and-forth can bump up against other deadlines in the contract.

What Happens If You Decline

If you decide not to agree to some or all of the requested repairs or credits, the buyer still retains whatever contingency rights are written into the purchase agreement. In practice, this usually means the buyer can choose to proceed without the repairs, continue negotiating, or cancel the contract within the contingency period and have their deposit returned per the agreement's terms. A flat refusal isn't necessarily the end of the deal, but it does put the decision back in the buyer's hands, so it's worth discussing the likely range of buyer reactions with your agent before responding.

Documenting Whatever Is Agreed

Whatever you and the buyer ultimately agree to — specific repairs, a credit amount, a price adjustment, or no changes at all — should be documented through a formal contract addendum rather than informal email or verbal agreement. This protects both sides and creates a clear record of what was promised, by when, and by whom, which matters at closing and afterward if any dispute arises about whether agreed work was completed.

Keeping Perspective

Repair negotiations can feel personal, especially when a buyer's list touches on something you've maintained carefully for years. It helps to remember that an inspection report is a structured, itemized document, and a buyer's agent is often advising their client to request everything reasonable as a starting point. Staying focused on the overall goal — closing the sale on terms that work for you — rather than any single line item tends to keep the negotiation productive.
